\\\"category\\\": \\\"related_chapter\\\", \\\"content\\\": \\\"[EXCERPT extracted-character range 0:4000]\\\\n# K-SYS-010：系统设计推导：把模型、缓存、执行与目标组合起来\\\\n\\\\n专家指导的产物不是一组彼此独立的优化提示，而是一条从任务条件到系统结构的可反驳推导链：状态模型、资源模型、候选设计、成本下界、证据状态和能区分竞争解释的实验。候选必须满足函数、身份、资源和完成条件，才有资格进入性能比较。下界通过只表示尚未被排除；上界未通过只表示尚未证明达标。两者都不能直接替代实际结果。\\\\n\\\\n## 统一问题表述：从条件到设计证书\\\\n\\\\n把设计条件写成 C＝(F,W,H,N,Q,S,E)。F 是模型函数、参数、位置规则、数值语义和必需状态；W 是到达过程、输入输出长度、前缀复用和会话依赖；H 是处理器、内存层级、互连、存储与拓扑；N 是运行时、编译器、驱动和可用执行路径；Q 是质量与数值容差；S 是首内容、逐 token、完成时间、吞吐、拒绝与公平目标；E 是已有来源事实、推导和测量及其作用域。设计变量 d 可以包含状态布局、缓存身份、调度粒度、执行后端、并行策略、阶段划分、队列和准入。\\\\n\\\\n输出不是单一总分，而是对每个条件格 k 和候选 d 给出设计证书：合法性、状态转移、各资源成本、证据支持的上下界、质量状态、排除理由，以及下一步区分实验。条件格是 F、W、H、N 的有限代表区域，例如模型版本、批大小、历史长度与共享或独立内存域的组合。格内连续变化的量仍须保留范围；中心点的结果不能自动覆盖整个格。\\\\n\\\\n设请求 r 的已知 token 数为 nᵣ，已提交且各必要层完整、可复用的 KV 终点为 cᵣ，满足 0≤cᵣ≤nᵣ。已生成文本不等于对应 KV 已计算；物理页已提交也不等于所有异步读者已经结束。系统在时刻 t 的驻留量为\\\\n\\\\nM(t)＝W_phys(t)＋Σ_unique P_state(t)＋A_work(t)＋I_flight(t)＋Q_queued(t)，\\\\n\\\\n其中 W_phys 是各物理副本的权重，P_state 是按存储域去重的状态页，A_work 是工作区，I_flight 是在途传输或暂定写，Q_queued 是消费者尚未释放的输出缓冲。同一物理 backing 在这些项间不重复计数。容量条件是 max_t M(t)≤M_cap；各项各自峰值之和只是保守上界，未必能在同一时刻达到。\\\\n\\\\n设计还必须固定比较的时间量 θ。它可以是某次固定执行的完成时间、预先指定有限回放的最大 ITL，或某个到达分布下的总体平均值、p99。它们是不同对象。下界、上界、观测和目标只有指向相同 θ，或存在明确的蕴含关系时，才能共同裁决候选。\\\\n\\\\n## 设计对象、合法性与证据状态\\\\n\\\\n合法性至少包含四层。函数合法性要求候选实现任务规定的模型函数、mask、位置、归一化和输出；数值合法性要求 dtype、累加、缩放、舍入和容差契约相容；设备语义要求布局、指令、可见性和完成事件支持所选路径；身份与并发合法性要求请求、版本、页、adapter、输出和迟到通知不会串用。任何一层失败都不能用平均更快抵消。允许近似的任务可以比较不同表示或求解轨迹，但必须把相应质量门槛写入 Q。\\\\n\\\\n普通稠密 GQA decoder 每 token 全层 KV 字节为\\\\n\\\\nb_KV＝2·L·H_kv·d_h·s，\\\\n\\\\nL 是层数，H_kv 是 KV head 数，d_h 是每 head 维数，s 是每元素字节。MLA 的持久 latent 不同，可按 L·(d_c＋d_Rh)·s 计算每 token 缓存主项。专家权重、临时分组激活、通信区与输出头另列。公式只描述声明的状态表示，不证明后端已选择相应 kernel。\\\\n\\\\n逻辑共享不等于物理共享，物理共享也不等于每次读取只发生一次。多个请求映射到同一物理前缀页时，容量账计一次；没有跨请求广播、片上驻留或其他复用契约时，各请求 attention 仍须取得自身可见历史，流量账不能直接去重。将共享页从流量中无证据扣除会低估带宽时间；把每次逻辑读取都当成新物理页又会高估容量。\\\\n\\\\n证书分别保存时间结论、质量状态与过期证据。下表的标签是主决策，原始证据及其他轴不因选择一个主标签而丢失。\\\\n\\\\n| 标签 | 含义与处理 | 不能推出 |\\\\n|---|---|---|\\\\n| `ILLEGAL_LEGALITY` | 已确认硬合法条件失败；排除当前候选与条件格的组合 | 修改表示或算法后的新候选也非法 |\\\\n| `ILLEGAL_CAPACITY` | 已确认该执行计划必需的峰值驻留超过容量 | 仅因一个宽松容量上界超预算就证明不可容纳 |\\\\n| `EXCLUDED_LOWER_BOUND` | 有效时间下界超过目标，且未发现同作用域矛盾证据 | 其他条件格也应排除 |\\\\n| `EXCLUDED_MEASURED` | 相应作用域的直接观测或获准统计证据支持时间失败 | 任意保守上界超过目标即可排除 |\\\\n| `EXCLUDED_QUALITY` | 同作用域质量证据判定失败；当前组合不能满足联合目标 | 提升速度能抵消质量失败 |\\\\n| `LOWER_BOUND_SURVIVOR` | 当前未证明失败，也未证明时间与质量全部通过；保留开放候选 | 已满足 SLO |\\\\n| `QUALITY_PENDING` | 时间已获支持通过，质量未知或质量证据过期；保留但不计为合格方案 | 可以省略质量评估 |\\\\n| `VERIFIED` | 同作用域时间与质量均按声明证据口径通过 | 其他形状、设备、负载或总体分位数也通过 |\\\\n| `EVIDENCE_STALE` | 尚开放，且存在不适用的时间或质量证据；记录失配字段 | 证据本身错误，或有效的其他排除证据失效 |\\\\n| `INCONSISTENT` | 对同一时间量的有效约束无共同解；转诊断并暂停相互矛盾证据的裁决效力 | 目标实现一定不可行 |\\\\n\\\\n质量采用 `pass`、`fail`、`unknown` 三态。未评估、区间不能裁决、任务分布改变或证据作用域失配都按 `unknown`；不能把没有发现质量错误解释为 `pass`。同作用域 `fail` 排除当前候选，`unknown` 保留候选但禁止 `VERIFIED`。质量评估依据可以是任务认可的独立数值参考、等价性论证或任务评估，具体范围必须记录。离线分类检查只消费这些状态，不生成真实模型质量结论。\\\\n\\\\n容量也要区分证明方向：精确计划峰值或必要驻留下界超容量可以排除；保守容量上界超过容量只说明该上界不能证明容纳。资源尚无法裁决时保留为资源待确认的开放候选。随章分类函数的布尔容量参数限定为容量已决的情况，不模拟这个未决阶段。\\\\n\\\\n## 上界、观测与统计口径怎样进入决策\\\\n\\\\n对固定候选与条件格，设目标为 θ≤τ，且已有有效下界 L。时间证据分三类。\\\\n\\\\n- 保守上界 U 声明 θ≤U。U≤τ 足以支持时间通过；U>τ 不说明 θ>τ。\\\\n- 直接观测 y 可以精确描述预先指定的有限执行或有限回放统计量，此时对那个有限对象有 θ=y。它不自动描述未来总体。\\\\n- 对总体均值或分位数的统计证据，应保留估计量、实验单位、区间 [a,b]、置信口径及方法假设。按预先声明的统计决策规则，b≤τ 支持通过，a>τ 支持失败，跨阈值则开放。点估计或样本最大值不能擅自变成总体硬上界。\\\\n\\\\n作用域至少核对模型及制品、表示和布局、backend、dtype、batch 与长度、缓存条件、资源域与并发、到达和拒绝口径、计时起止、目标统计量及其人群。计时误差也要进入观测区间。将多个统计区间共同使用前，须说明联合覆盖或决策规则；分别名义 95% 的区间不能无说明地拼成一个确定证书。[性能实验](../tools/statistical-experiments.md)进一步区分运行、请求与环境重复。\\\\n\\\\n把适用证据与下界相交，得到\\\\n\\\\nL*＝max(L, 所有适用观测区间的下端)，\\\\n\\\\nU*＝min(所有适用保守上界及观测区间的上端)，\\\\n\\\\n没有上端证据时 U*＝＋∞。若 L*>U*，先进入 `INCONSISTENT`，即使 L 已超过目标也不能提前按它排除。这里的矛盾表示各前提或区间不能同时采用；对于统计区间，它还可能暴露覆盖失败或方法不适用，不能立即断言硬件违反物理定律。\\\\n\\\\n宽松上界的反例是 L＝39.0625 ms、U＝80 ms、τ＝60 ms。实际值可以为 50 ms，同时满足 L≤50≤U 和目标；仅凭这组界必须保留候选。反过来，若已有同作用域有效上界 55 ms，而声明下界为 70 ms、目标为 60 ms，先排除会错删一个可能通过的方案。正确动作是保存冲突，检查单位、资源能力、缓存前提和计时边界，修正证据后重新分类。\\\\n\\\\n若时间上界 55 ms 通过目标 60 ms，但质量为 `fail`，结果是 `EXCLUDED_QUALITY`；质量为 `unknown` 时是 `QUALITY_PENDING`；只有质量为有效 `pass` 才能成为 `VERIFIED`。这三个分支不要求离线检查执行真实模型评估。\\\\n\\\\n## 完整推导算法：候选、条件格与证据更新\\\\n\\\\n以下算法串联条件、合法性、容量、下界、观测、质量与下一实验。候选族可以来自参数化搜索、已有实现或人工设计。已有测量可以先于解析推导取得，不要求研发按伪代码的论证顺序施工。\\\\n\\\\n```pseudocode\\\\n算法 SYNTHESIZE(C,D,budget)\\\\n输入：C=(F,W,H,N,Q,S,E)；候选族 D；实验预算\\\\n输出：逐格设计证书、保留候选与下一实验，或明确的空集原因\\\\n\\\\n1 归一化单位、逻辑轴、目标统计量和时间窗；将条件划分为有限格 K\\\\n  若 K 为空，报告缺少目标条件；若 D 为空，报告没有候选\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n[EXCERPT extracted-character range 8000:14625]\\\\natch 需同时计算路径、排队、偏斜与接收端容量。若做 prefill/decode 分离，还需计状态传输、分片转换和完整提交。较小 KV 不等于网络免费，也不意味着专家热点解决。\\\\n\\\\n区分实验可以固定模型和请求，只改变 EP 度数，记录每链路字节、专家最大负载及尾延迟；固定 EP、只改变 TP，记录本地分片与归约时间；固定并行计划、改变路由或共享前缀，观察队列和流量是否按预测变化。训练时的路由均衡目标不保证每次推理严格均衡。若实际干预同时改变副本、路由和 batch，需要拆开或记录这些中介变化，不能用一个平均吞吐裁决所有解释。\\\\n\\\\n## 场景四：静态编译平台上的混合长度任务\\\\n\\\\n模型函数固定而服务形状变化时，可按 prompt、query、context 和 batch 的联合分布选择有限桶。设备保留 KV，控制面推进真实长度；越界走明确回退、较粗桶或拒绝，不能静默截断。编译准备、executable、workspace 和图池驻留共同进入启动与容量预算。\\\\n\\\\n前缀命中改变待算 query 分布，连续批改变 batch 分布，投机改变验证长度分布。桶选择应在这些机制组合后的 workload 上推导。命中后 query 变短、host 固定成本上升时，大 decode 桶未必优于专门小桶；长请求比例上升后，粗桶的 padding 和 KV 驻留又会改变比较。\\\\n\\\\n固定 NxD Inference 文档的前缀缓存路径先 gather 块 KV，再转换到 flat 布局计算，最后 scatter 回去；这说明支持共享状态不等于直接使用 PagedAttention。布局转换的准备、读取、写入与驻留要进入该候选，不能把另一 backend 的流量模型直接移植过来。\\\\n\\\\n## 组合轨迹：CPU 多请求生成的完整推导\\\\n\\\\n以下参数全部是可复算设定，不是目标机器或模型实测。任务是固定版本稠密 GQA decoder 文本生成，质量由独立固定前缀 forward 与任务评估判定。8 个活跃交互请求，平均外部到达 2 请求/s，每请求生成 64 token，平均输入 512 token，缓存计算历史上限 2048。客户端 ITL 目标为 60 ms；主机与响应预算暂设 4 ms，真实排队和网络是否满足仍需测量。\\\\n\\\\n硬件设定为一个 32 核、32 GiB 可用主存服务域，主存读带宽模型参数为 96 GiB/s；权重与已选布局合计 3 GiB，固定和临时工作区预算 2 GiB。状态参数为 24 层、4 个 KV head、head_dim＝128、每元素 2 字节。dtype、累加与指令路径仍须由实现确认，不能由权重大小推断。\\\\n\\\\n### 模型与容量\\\\n\\\\n每 token 全层 KV 为 2×24×4×128×2＝49,152 字节，即 48 KiB。2048 token 历史为每请求 96 MiB；8 请求为 768 MiB，权重＋工作区＋KV 为 5.75 GiB，另需页尾、输入输出、在途与保留余量。64 个同长请求的主项为 11 GiB；这只说明所列项未超容量。同域两副本各复制 3 GiB 权重与 2 GiB 工作区，再加总计 0.75 GiB KV，主项为 10.75 GiB。\\\\n\\\\n加载按 [制品与布局](../frameworks/checkpoint-loading.md) 建立固定参数，避免不必要的完整转换副本。[分配器](memory-allocators.md)管理请求状态；初版不必使用共享前缀或分页，连续池与固定块池也可保持相同模型语义，应比较长短混合下的碎片和增长。已输出 token 与已计算 KV 的边界分别记录。\\\\n\\\\n### 三个执行候选\\\\n\\\\n| 候选 | 推进组织 | 主要收益与代价 |\\\\n|---|---|---|\\\\n| A：逐请求单独执行 | 每次一个请求推进一个 token，再轮转 | 路径简单，权重在请求间重复读取 |\\\\n| B：单实例连续批 | 同轮合并 8 个就绪 decode，prefill 受时间预算约束 | 摊薄权重读取，需要批次身份、状态与公平调度 |\\\\n| C：同域两个副本 | 每实例处理 4 个 decode | 隔离请求，复制权重与工作区，竞争同域带宽 |\\\\n\\\\n在每次调用读取全部 3 GiB 权重、每请求读取全历史 KV、忽略其他流量的设定下，A 一次流量为 3.09375 GiB，带宽下界约 32.23 ms；8 请求轮转一次约 257.81 ms，无法支持各请求 60 ms 的间隔。B 一轮为 3.75 GiB，下界为 39.0625 ms，相应理想吞吐上界为 204.8 输出 token/s。\\\\n\\\\nC 均分同域带宽时，每实例 48 GiB/s，流量 3.375 GiB，下界为 70.3125 ms，超过目标。两个实例各有独立 96 GiB/s 带宽域时，下界则为 35.15625 ms。副本是否共享资源必须成为条件格；独立域的选择反转也不证明真实时间已通过。\\\\n\\\\n64 请求全进一轮时，权重加 KV 为 9 GiB，下界为 93.75 ms。内存容得下与 ITL 达标是两回事；轮转成多个小批仍有等待其他轮次的时间，admission 不能只按内存上限设置。若目标观测与这些下界冲突，先核对权重是否真的每轮从主存读完、历史读取层级和带宽设定，再作排除。\\\\n\\\\n### 将 prefill、主机和质量接入同一方案\\\\n\\\\n对 B，60−4−39.0625＝16.9375 ms 是理想 decode 下界之外的预算差，不保证真实实现仍有这些余量。计算、额外事务和同步可能先消耗它。需要测混合批时间曲面，再按 [分块 prefill](../algorithms/chunked-prefill.md)选择合法块；所有块均不满足时应调整运行点、准入或资源。\\\\n\\\\n平均到达产生 128 输出 token/s，低于上述理想上界，但还要承担每秒 1024 个新输入 token 的 prefill，所以不能据此断言稳定。分词、调度、响应与输出队列有独立成本和容量；慢客户端、取消与迟到完成都要回传到资源责任账。\\\\n\\\\nCPU 线性层比较无打包与预打包、线程数和 M 形态。B 每轮 M 约为 8，同一权重行可服务多请求。沿输出通道分线程可避免最终归约，沿 K 分线程需要部分和、工作区及同步。线程增多同时改变并行度、NUMA、cache 和争用；主存模型不证明线程越多越快。低位权重还需区分同量化制品的执行正确性和相对原模型的任务质量；字节下降后应重算资源账，不能直接乘理论压缩倍数。\\\\n\\\\n### 一次组合状态轨迹\\\\n\\\\n1. 准入计算唯一 KV、权重、工作区及增长、页尾、输出余量。容量预留不证明 ITL；预留池与池内物化页不重复相加。\\\\n2. 选择 8 个就绪 decode，为各请求保留可写尾页与输出槽，建立不可变执行视图，绑定请求生命期、逻辑位置、页映射、结果槽和轮次。共享尾页追加前按所选 COW 方案取得独占写区。\\\\n3. 按视图读取权重与各请求历史；39.0625 ms 仍是条件化下界。没有时间上界或有效观测时，候选只处于开放状态；质量也可能尚未知。\\\\n4. 完成通知核对轮次与代次，确认必要写入和结果读取达到完成边界，再提交 KV 前沿。到达已知前缀末行、确有合法 logits 且仍有生成配额时，才采样一次；输出按请求和序号入队。\\\\n5. 完整 KV 命中却没有末行 logits 时，不得因待算长度为零而永久等待。可以安全重算最后一个已知 token：逐层读取此前历史、在私有暂存计算当前行，不覆盖共享页；也可以使用绑定相同模型与前缀的有效 logits 缓存。已确认输出重放不再次采样。\\\\n6. 取消阻止未来业务提交，但不提前释放设备仍读取的页。读者结束后再降低相应执行引用；迟到通知只结算旧轮次，不写回新视图或下一生命期。\\\\n7. 若取得 80 ms 的保守客户端 ITL 上界，不能因它超过 60 ms 就排除 B，39.0625 到 80 ms 之间仍含满足目标的值。应收紧上界或取得同作用域观测。\\\\n8. 假设某个预先固定的有限回放，其客户端 ITL 最大值测为 55 ms，且计时含主机、排队与交付边界，该证据只证明该回放时间通过。质量 `pass` 才可在这个有限作用域标为 `VERIFIED`；质量 `fail` 排除，`unknown` 保留待验。该 55 ms 不能直接证明总体 p99 或每次未来请求通过。\\\\n\\\\n上述轨迹不包含真实 CPU 性能计数器或 GPU 测量。真实时间受 cache/TLB、事务、线程调度、同步、网络和负载影响，质量需要另行评估。\\\\n\\\\n### 区分实验与反转条件\\\\n\\\\n先用独立固定前缀参考比较完整、分块与增量 forward，再改变 batch 排列、物理槽位、跨页和取消后复用。输出身份与采样状态分别检查；最终字符串相同不足以证明资源回收或取消正确。\\\\n\\\\n性能实验扫描活跃数、历史、prefill 块、线程和副本，记录实际流量、阶段时间、TTFT/ITL、拒绝、超时与队列增长。首次加载和稳态分开，在独立运行或预定区组保留验证。低负载单请求时 A 可能更合适；独立 NUMA 域资源足够时 C 的隔离价值可能占优；长历史主导流量时 batch 的权重摊薄收益下降；离线且放宽 ITL 时可比较更大批与粗 prefill。改变条件后保留状态不变量，重算成本并重新取得适用证据。\\\\n\\\\n## 十二类完整场景如何连成知识体系\\\\n\\\\n设计场景将各章机制放进共同任务边界。以下入口给出条件化候选与资源推导，不表示目标硬件已经完成性能实验。先固定任务函数、质量与服务边界，再选择路径。\\\\n\\\\n| 任务形态 | 完整场景入口 | 需要一起检验的关系 |\\\\n|---|---|---|\\\\n| C01 CPU 多请求生成 | 本章 CPU 场景 | 权重/KV 流量、线程与 prefill 时间片、开放到达和 ITL |\\\\n| C02 单 GPU 交互 | [CUDA 平台](../hardware/cuda-execution.md) | 容量、带宽、内核与主机间隙、准入和输出 |\\\\n| C03 长上下文高复用 | [前缀缓存](../algorithms/prefix-cache-identity.md) | 物理共享容量、逻辑读取、路由与长尾 |\\\\n| C04 显存不足与三级存储 | [多级驻留](../algorithms/tiered-residency.md) | 有效副本、预取、共享带宽、双缓冲与恢复 |\\\\n| C05 CPU–GPU 混合执行 | [异构计算](../algorithms/heterogeneous-execution.md) | 计算放置、传输路径、合并与主机竞争 |\\\\n| C06 多卡 MLA/MoE | [多设备并行](../algorithms/parallelism.md) | 逐 rank 容量、head/latent/专家归属、通信与偏斜 |\\\\n| C07 P/D 与远端 KV | [分离服务](../algorithms/disaggregated-serving.md) | 首内容、第二 token、迁移提交与池配比 |\\\\n| C08 多模型/LoRA | [多模型放置](../workloads/multi-model-placement.md) | 共同基座、adapter/KV、冷加载与租户等待 |\\\\n| C09 流式语音 | [转写](../models/encoder-decoder-streaming.md)、[语音生成](../models/speech-generation.md) | 稳定文字、可播放音频、阶段状态与消费时钟 |\\\\n| C10 VLM/全模态 | Chun∗\\\\nFriendliAI\\\\nSeoul National University\\\\nAbstract\\\\nLarge-scale Transformer-based models trained for generation\\\\ntasks (e.g., GPT-3) have recently attracted huge interest, em-\\\\nphasizing the need for system support for serving models in\\\\nthis family. Since these models generate a next token in an au-\\\\ntoregressive manner, one has to run the model multiple times\\\\nto process an inference request where each iteration of the\\\\nmodel generates a single output token for the request. How-\\\\never, existing systems for inference serving do not perform\\\\nwell on this type of workload that has a multi-iteration char-\\\\nacteristic, due to their inﬂexible scheduling mechanism that\\\\ncannot change the current batch of requests being processed;\\\\nrequests that have ﬁnished earlier than other requests in a\\\\nbatch cannot return to the client, while newly arrived requests\\\\nhave to wait until the current batch completely ﬁnishes.\\\\nIn this paper, we propose iteration-level scheduling, a new\\\\nscheduling mechanism that schedules execution at the gran-\\\\nularity of iteration (instead of request) where the scheduler\\\\ninvokes the execution engine to run only a single iteration of\\\\nthe model on the batch. In addition, to apply batching and\\\\niteration-level scheduling to a Transformer model at the same\\\\ntime, we suggest selective batching, which applies batching\\\\nonly to a selected set of operations. Based on these two tech-\\\\nniques, we have implemented a distributed serving system\\\\ncalled ORCA, with additional designs for scalability to models\\\\nwith hundreds of billions of parameters. Our evaluation on a\\\\nGPT-3 175B model shows that ORCA can signiﬁcantly out-\\\\nperform NVIDIA FasterTransformer in terms of both latency\\\\nand throughput: 36.9× throughput improvement at the same\\\\nlevel of latency.\\\\n1\\\\nIntroduction\\\\nLanguage generation tasks are becoming increasingly\\\\nparamount to many types of applications, such as chatbot [9,\\\\n52], summarization [41,45,54], code generation [13], and cap-\\\\ntion generation [65,66]. Moreover, recent works published by\\\\n∗Corresponding author.\\\\nAI21 Labs [37], DeepMind [26,48], Google [15,21,63], Meta\\\\nPlatforms [10,67], Microsoft [50], Microsoft & NVIDIA [59],\\\\nand OpenAI [12] have reported that every language process-\\\\ning task, including translation [11,17], classiﬁcation [20,53],\\\\nquestion-answering [32, 33, 40] and more, can be cast as a\\\\nlanguage generation problem and have shown great improve-\\\\nments along this direction. The rise of generative models is\\\\nnot limited to the language domain; the AI community has\\\\nalso given growing interest to generation problems in other do-\\\\nmains such as image, video, speech, or a mixture of multiple\\\\ndomains [19,38,51,62]. At the heart of generative models lies\\\\nthe Transformer architecture [60] and its variants [15,47–49].\\\\nBy relying on the attention mechanism [60], Transformer\\\\nmodels can learn better representations where each element\\\\nof the sequence may have a direct connection with every other\\\\nelement, which was not possible in recurrent models [25].\\\\nTo use generative models in real-world applications, we\\\\noften delegate the inference procedure to a separate service\\\\nresponsible for ML inference serving. The growing demands\\\\nfor this service, which should provide inference results for\\\\nclient requests at low latency and high throughput, have fa-\\\\ncilitated the development of inference serving systems such\\\\nas Triton Inference Server [7] and TensorFlow Serving [42].\\\\nThese systems can use a separately-developed DNN execution\\\\nengine to perform the actual tensor operations. For example,\\\\nwe can deploy a service for language generation tasks by\\\\nusing a combination of Triton and FasterTransformer [4], an\\\\nexecution engine optimized for the inference of Transformer-\\\\nbased models. In this case, Triton is mainly responsible for\\\\ngrouping multiple client requests into a batch, while Faster-\\\\nTransformer receives the batch from Triton and conducts the\\\\ninference procedure in the batched manner.\\\\nUnfortunately, we notice that the existing inference sys-\\\\ntems, including both the serving system layer and the execu-\\\\ntion engine layer, have limitations in handling requests for\\\\nTransformer-based generative models. Since these models are\\\\ntrained to generate a next token in an autoregressive manner,\\\\none should run the model as many times as the number of to-\\\\nkens to generate, while for other models like ResNet [24] and\\\\nUSENIX Association\\\\n16th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation    521\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 3 ---\\\\nBERT [18] a request can be processed by running the model\\\\nonce. That is, in order to process a request to the generative\\\\nmodel, we have to run multiple iterations of the model; each\\\\niteration generates a single output token, which is used as\\\\nan input in the following iteration. Such multi-iteration char-\\\\nacteristic calls into question the current design of inference\\\\nsystems, where the serving system schedules the execution\\\\nof the engine at the granularity of request. Under this design,\\\\nwhen the serving system dispatches a batch of requests to\\\\nthe engine, the engine returns inference results for the entire\\\\nbatch at once after processing all requests within the batch.\\\\nAs different client requests may require different numbers of\\\\niterations for processing, requests that have ﬁnished earlier\\\\nthan others in the batch cannot return to the client, resulting\\\\nin an increased latency. Requests arrived after dispatching the\\\\nbatch also should wait for processing the batch, which can\\\\nsigniﬁcantly increase the requests’ queueing time.\\\\nIn this paper, we propose to schedule the execution of the\\\\nengine at the granularity of iteration instead of request. In\\\\nparticular, the serving system invokes the engine to run only a\\\\nsingle iteration of the model on the batch. As a result, a newly\\\\narrived request can be considered for processing after waiting\\\\nfor only a single iteration of the model. The serving system\\\\nchecks whether a request has ﬁnished processing after every\\\\nreturn from the engine – hence the ﬁnished requests can also\\\\nbe returned to the clients immediately.\\\\nNevertheless, a noticeable challenge arises when we at-\\\\ntempt to apply batching and the iteration-level scheduling at\\\\nthe same time. Unlike the canonical request-level scheduling,\\\\nthe proposed scheduling can issue a batch of requests where\\\\neach request has so far processed a different number of tokens.\\\\nIn such a case, the requests to the Transformer model cannot\\\\nbe processed in the batched manner because the attention\\\\nmechanism calls for non-batchable tensor operations whose\\\\ninput tensors have variable shapes depending on the number\\\\nof processed tokens.\\\\nTo address this challenge, we suggest to apply batching\\\\nonly to a selected set of operations, which we call selective\\\\nbatching. By taking different characteristics of operations into\\\\naccount, selective batching splits the batch and processes each\\\\nrequest individually for the Attention1 operation while apply-\\\\ning batching to other operations of the Transformer model.\\\\nWe observe that the decision not to batch the executions of\\\\nthe Attention operation has only a small impact on efﬁciency.\\\\nSince the Attention operation is not associated with any model\\\\nparameters, applying batching to Attention has no beneﬁt of\\\\nreducing the amount of GPU memory reads by reusing the\\\\nloaded parameters across multiple requests.\\\\nBased on these techniques, we design and implement\\\\nORCA, a distributed serving system for Transformer-based\\\\ngenerative models. In order to handle large-scale models,\\\\n1In some literature the Attention operation has an extended deﬁnition that\\\\nincludes linear layers (QKV Linear and Attn Out Linear; Figure 1b). On the\\\\nother hand, we use a narrow deﬁnition as described in Figure 1b.\\\\nORCA adopts parallelization strategies including intra-layer\\\\nand inter-layer model parallelism, which were originally de-\\\\nveloped by training systems [55,58] for Transformer models.\\\\nWe also devise a new scheduling algorithm for the proposed\\\\niteration-level scheduling, with additional considerations for\\\\nmemory management and pipelined execution across work-\\\\ners.\\\\nWe evaluate ORCA using OpenAI GPT-3 [12] models with\\\\nvarious conﬁgurations, scaling up to 341B of parameters. The\\\\nresults show that ORCA signiﬁcantly outperforms FasterTrans-\\\\nformer [4], showing 36.9× throughput improvement at the\\\\nsame level of latency. While we use a language model as\\\\na driving example throughout the paper and conduct experi-\\\\nments only on language models, generative models in other\\\\ndomains can beneﬁt from our approach as long as the mod-\\\\nels are based on the Transformer architecture and use the\\\\nautoregressive generation procedure [19,38,51,62].\\\\n2\\\\nBackground\\\\nWe provide background on the inference procedure of\\\\nGPT [12,47], a representative example of Transformer-based\\\\ngenerative models that we use throughout this paper, and ML\\\\ninference serving systems.\\\\nInference procedure of GPT.\\\\nGPT is an autoregressive\\\\nlanguage model based on one of architectural variants of\\\\nTransformer [60]. It takes text as input and produces new text\\\\nas output. In particular, the model receives a sequence of input\\\\ntokens and then completes the sequence by generating subse-\\\\nquent output tokens. Figure 1a illustrates a simpliﬁed compu-\\\\ntation graph that represents this procedure with a three-layer\\\\nGPT model, where nodes and edges indicate Transformer\\\\nlayers and dependencies between the layers, respectively. The\\\\nTransformer layers are executed in the order denoted by the\\\\nnumbers on the nodes, and the nodes that use the same set\\\\nof model parameters (i.e., nodes representing the same layer)\\\\nare ﬁlled with the same color.\\\\nThe generated output token is fed back into the model to\\\\ngenerate the next output token, imposing a sequential, one-\\\\nby-one inference procedure. This autoregressive procedure of\\\\ngenerating a single token is done by running all the layers of\\\\nthe model with the input, which is either a sequence of input\\\\ntokens that came from the client or a previously generated out-\\\\nput token. We deﬁne the run of all layers as an iteration of the\\\\nmodel. In the example shown in Figure 1a, the inference pro-\\\\ncedure comprises three iterations. The ﬁrst iteration (“iter 1”)\\\\ntakes all the input tokens (“I think this”) at once and generates\\\\nthe next token (“is”). This iteration composes an initiation\\\\nphase, a procedure responsible for processing the input tokens\\\\nand generating the ﬁrst output token. Note that while the increment\\\\nphase comprises multiple iterations because each iteration\\\\nis only able to process a single token, the initiation phase is\\\\ntypically implemented as a single iteration by processing all\\\\nthe input tokens in parallel.\\\\nThe original Transformer [60] employs two stacks of Trans-\\\\nformer layers, while GPT’s architecture consists of a single\\\\nlayer stack, namely decoder. Figure 1b shows a Transformer\\\\nlayer used in GPT. Among the operations that compose the\\\\nTransformer layer, Attention is the essence that distinguishes\\\\nTransformer from other architectures. At a high level, the At-\\\\ntention operation computes a weighted average of the tokens\\\\nof interest so that each token in the sequence is aware of the\\\\nother. It takes three inputs, query, key, and value, computes dot\\\\nproducts of the query (for the current token) with all keys (for\\\\nthe tokens of interest), applies Softmax on the dot products\\\\nto get weights, and conducts weighted average of all values\\\\nassociated with the weights.\\\\nSince the Attention requires keys and values of all pre-\\\\nceding tokens,2 we consider the keys and values as internal\\\\nstates that should be maintained across multiple iterations. A\\\\nnaïve, state-less inference procedure would take all tokens in\\\\nthe sequence (including both the client-provided input tokens\\\\nand the output tokens generated so far) to recompute all the\\\\nkeys and values at every iteration. To avoid such recomputa-\\\\ntion, fairseq [43] suggests incremental decoding, which saves\\\\nthe keys and values for reuse in successive iterations. Other\\\\nsystems for Transformer such as FasterTransformer [4] and\\\\nMegatron-LM [3] also do the same.\\\\n2Language models like GPT use causal masking, which means all pre-\\\\nceding tokens are of interest and participate in the Attention operation.\\\\nFigure 1c illustrates the state usage pattern of Transformer,\\\\nalong with LSTM [25] that also maintains internal states. The\\\\nmain difference is that the size of the states (k for Attention\\\\nkey and v for value) in Transformer increases with iteration,\\\\nwhereas the size of the states (c for LSTM internal memory\\\\nand h for LSTM layer’s input/output) in LSTM remains con-\\\\nstant. When processing the token at index t, the Attention\\\\noperation takes all previous Attention keys kl,1:t−1 and values\\\\nvl,1:t−1 along with the current key kl,t and value vl,t.3 There-\\\\nfore, the Attention operation should perform computation on\\\\ntensors of different shapes depending on the number of tokens\\\\nalready processed.\\\\nPrior to the Attention operation, there are the layer normal-\\\\nization operation (LayerNorm) and the QKV Linear (linear\\\\nand split operations to get the query, key and value). Opera-\\\\ntions performed after Attention are, in order, a linear operation\\\\n(Attn Out Linear), an add operation for residual connection\\\\n(Add), layer normalization operation (LayerNorm), the multi-\\\\nlayer perceptron (MLP) operations, and the other residual\\\\nconnection operation (Add).\\\\nML inference serving systems.\\\\nGrowing demands for ML-\\\\ndriven applications have made ML inference serving service\\\\na critical workload in modern datacenters. In particular, the service\\\\nruns a DNN model with input data to generate output for the\\\\n3kl,1:t−1 represents Attention keys of the l-th layer for tokens at indices\\\\n1 to t −1 while kl,t is for the Attention key of the l-th layer for the token at\\\\nindex t. Just like other services operating on datacenters, a\\\\nwell-managed inference service should provide low latency\\\\nand high throughput within a reasonable amount of cost.\\\\nTo meet such constraints, service operators often use ML\\\\ninference serving systems such as Triton Inference Server [7]\\\\nand TensorFlow Serving [42]. These systems can be seen as\\\\nan abstraction sitting atop underlying model execution en-\\\\ngines such as TensorRT [6], TVM [14], TensorFlow [8], and\\\\nmany others [44,46], being agnostic to various kinds of ML\\\\nmodels, execution engines, and computing hardware. While\\\\ndelegating the role of driving the main mathematical opera-\\\\ntions to the engines, serving systems are in charge of exposing\\\\nendpoints that receive inference requests, scheduling execu-\\\\ntions of the engine, and sending responses to the requests.\\\\nAccordingly, these systems focus on aspects such as batch-\\\\ning the executions [7,16,35,42,56], selecting an appropriate\\\\nmodel from multiple model variants [16,27,30,57], deploying\\\\nmultiple models (each for different inference services) on the\\\\nsame device [7,29,35,56], and so on.\\\\nAmong the features and optimizations provided by serv-\\\\ning systems, batching is a key to achieve high accelerator\\\\nutilization when using accelerators like GPUs. When we run\\\\nthe execution engine with batching enabled, the input tensors\\\\nfrom multiple requests coalesce into a single, large input ten-\\\\nsor before being fed to the ﬁrst operation of the model. Since\\\\nthe accelerators prefer large input tensors over small ones to\\\\nbetter exploit the vast amount of parallel computation units,\\\\nthe engine’s throughput is highly dependent on the batch size,\\\\ni.e., the number of inference requests the engine processes\\\\ntogether. Reusing the model parameters loaded from off-chip\\\\nmemory is another merit in batched execution, especially\\\\nwhen the model involves memory-intensive operations.\\\\nFigure 2 shows an overall workﬂow of serving a generative\\\\nlanguage model with existing serving systems and execution\\\\nengines. The main component of the serving system (e.g., Tri-\\\\nton [7]) is the scheduler, which is responsible for  creating\\\\na batch of requests by retrieving requests from a queue and \\\\nscheduling the execution engine (e.g., FasterTransformer [4])\\\\nto process the batch. The execution engine  processes the\\\\nreceived batch by running multiple iterations of the model\\\\nbeing served and  returns the generated text back to the\\\\nserving system. In Figure 2, the serving system schedules the\\\\nengine to process two requests (x1: “I think”, x2: “I love”) in\\\\niter 1\\\\nx1\\\\nx1\\\\nx2\\\\nx2\\\\niter 2\\\\nI\\\\nthink\\\\nI\\\\nlove\\\\nthis\\\\nyou\\\\nthis\\\\nyou\\\\niter 3\\\\nis\\\\n-\\\\nis\\\\n<EOS>\\\\ngreat\\\\n-\\\\niter 4\\\\ngreat\\\\n-\\\\n<EOS>\\\\n-\\\\nFigure 3: An illustration for a case where the requests have the\\\\nsame input length but some requests ﬁnish earlier than others.\\\\nShaded tokens represent input tokens. “-” denotes inputs and\\\\noutputs of extra computation imposed by the scheduling.\\\\na batch and the engine generates “this is great” and “you” for\\\\nrequests x1 and x2, respectively.\\\\n3\\\\nChallenges and Proposed Solutions\\\\nIn this section, we describe challenges in serving Transformer-\\\\nbased generative models and propose two techniques:\\\\niteration-level scheduling and selective batching.\\\\nC1: Early-ﬁnished and late-joining requests.\\\\nOne major\\\\nlimitation of existing systems is that the serving system and\\\\nthe execution engine interact with each other only when (1)\\\\nthe serving system schedules the next batch on an idle engine;\\\\nor (2) the engine ﬁnishes processing the current batch. In\\\\nother words, these systems are designed to schedule execu-\\\\ntions at request granularity; the engine maintains a batch of\\\\nrequests ﬁxed until all requests in the batch ﬁnish. This can be\\\\nproblematic in the serving of generative models, since each\\\\nrequest in a batch may require different number of iterations,\\\\nresulting in certain requests ﬁnishing earlier than the others.\\\\nIn the example shown in Figure 3, although request x2 ﬁnishes\\\\nearlier than request x1, the engine performs computation for\\\\nboth “active” and “inactive” requests throughout all iterations.\\\\nSuch extra computation for inactive requests (x2 at iter 3 and\\\\n4) limits the efﬁciency of batched execution.\\\\nWhat makes it even worse is that this behavior prevents an\\\\nearly return of the ﬁnished request to the client, imposing a\\\\nsubstantial amount of extra latency. This is because the engine\\\\nonly returns the execution results to the serving system when\\\\nit ﬁnishes processing all requests in the batch. Similarly, when\\\\na new request arrives in the middle of the current batch’s\\\\nexecution, the aforementioned scheduling mechanism makes\\\\nthe newly arrived request wait until all requests in the current\\\\nbatch have ﬁnished. We argue that the current request-level\\\\nscheduling mechanism cannot efﬁciently handle workloads\\\\nwith multi-iteration characteristic. Note that this problem of\\\\nearly-ﬁnished and late-joining requests does not occur in the\\\\ntraining of language models; the training procedure ﬁnishes\\\\nprocessing the whole batch in a single iteration by using the\\\\nteacher forcing technique [64].\\\\n524    16th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation\\\\nUSENIX Association\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 6 ---\\\\nresponse\\\\nOrca System\\\\nEndpoint\\\\nrequest\\\\nScheduler\\\\nRequest Pool\\\\nExecution\\\\nEngine\\\\n!\\\\n\\\\\\\"\\\\n#\\\\nx1\\\\nx1 x11\\\\nx11 x12\\\\nx12 x13\\\\nx13 x14\\\\nx14\\\\nx2\\\\nx2 x21\\\\nx21 x22\\\\nx22\\\\nx3\\\\nx3 x31\\\\nx31 x32\\\\nx32\\\\nx4\\\\nx4 x41\\\\nx41 x42\\\\nx42 x43\\\\nx43\\\\nx1, x2, x3, x4\\\\nx1, x2, x3, x4\\\\n· · ·\\\\n· · ·\\\\nx15, x23, x33, x44\\\\nx15, x23, x33, x44\\\\n$\\\\nFigure 4: System overview of ORCA. Interactions between\\\\ncomponents represented as dotted lines indicate that the inter-\\\\naction takes place at every iteration of the execution engine.\\\\nxi j is the j-th token of the i-th request. Shaded tokens repre-\\\\nsent input tokens received from the clients, while unshaded\\\\ntokens are generated by ORCA. For example, request x1 ini-\\\\ntially arrived with two input tokens (x11,x12) and have run\\\\ntwo iterations so far, where the ﬁrst and second iterations gen-\\\\nerated x13 and x14, respectively. On the other hand, request\\\\nx3 only contains input tokens (x31,x32) because it has not run\\\\nany iterations yet.\\\\nS1: Iteration-level scheduling.\\\\nTo address the above limi-\\\\ntations, we propose to schedule executions at the granularity\\\\nof iteration. At high level, the scheduler repeats the follow-\\\\ning procedure: (1) selects requests to run next; (2) invokes\\\\nthe engine to execute one iteration for the selected requests;\\\\nand (3) receives execution results for the scheduled iteration.\\\\nSince the scheduler receives a return on every iteration, it can\\\\ndetect the completion of a request and immediately return its\\\\ngenerated tokens to the client. For a newly arrived request, the\\\\nrequest gets a chance to start processing (i.e., the scheduler\\\\nmay select the new request to run next) after execution of\\\\nthe currently scheduled iteration, signiﬁcantly reducing the\\\\nqueueing delay. With iteration-level scheduling, the sched-\\\\nuler has a full control on how many and which requests are\\\\nprocessed in each iteration.\\\\nFigure 4 depicts the system architecture and the overall\\\\nworkﬂow of ORCA using the iteration-level scheduling. ORCA\\\\nexposes an endpoint (e.g., HTTPS or gRPC) where inference\\\\nrequests arrive at the system and responses to the requests\\\\nare sent out. The endpoint puts newly arrived requests in the\\\\nrequest pool, a component that manages all requests in the\\\\nsystem during their lifetime. The pool is monitored by the\\\\nscheduler, which is responsible for: selecting a set of requests\\\\nfrom the pool, scheduling the execution engine to run an it-\\\\neration of the model on the set, receiving execution results\\\\n(i.e., output tokens) from the engine, and updating the pool\\\\nby appending each output token to the corresponding request.\\\\nThe engine is an abstraction for executing the actual tensor\\\\noperations, which can be parallelized across multiple GPUs\\\\nspread across multiple machines. In the example shown in\\\\nFigure 4, the scheduler  interacts with the request pool to\\\\ndecide which requests to run next and  invokes the engine\\\\nto run four selected requests: (x1,x2,x3,x4). The scheduler\\\\nprovides the engine with input tokens of the requests sched-\\\\nuled for the ﬁrst time. In this case, x3 and x4 have not run\\\\nany iterations yet, so the scheduler hands over (x31,x32) for\\\\nx3 and (x41,x42,x43) for x4. The engine  runs an iteration\\\\nof the model on the four requests and  returns generated\\\\noutput tokens (x15,x23,x33,x44), one for each scheduled re-\\\\nquest. Once a request has ﬁnished processing, the request pool\\\\nremoves the ﬁnished request and notiﬁes the endpoint to send\\\\na response. Unlike the method shown in Figure 2 that should\\\\nrun multiple iterations on a scheduled batch until ﬁnish of\\\\nall requests within the batch, ORCA’s scheduler can change\\\\nwhich requests are going to be processed at every iteration.\\\\nWe describe the detailed algorithm about how to select the\\\\nrequests at every iteration in Section 4.2.\\\\nC2: Batching an arbitrary set of requests.\\\\nWhen we try\\\\nto use the iteration-level scheduling in practice, one major\\\\nchallenge that we are going to face is batching. To achieve\\\\nhigh efﬁciency, the execution engine should be able to process\\\\nany selected set of requests in the batched manner. Without\\\\nbatching, one would have to process each selected request\\\\none by one, losing out on the massively parallel computation\\\\ncapabilities of GPUs.\\\\nUnfortunately, there is no guarantee that even for a pair of\\\\nrequests (xi,xj), for the next iteration, their executions can be\\\\nmerged and replaced with a batched version. There are three\\\\ncases for a pair of requests where the next iteration cannot\\\\nbe batched together: (1) both requests are in the initiation\\\\nphase and each has different number of input tokens (e.g.,\\\\nx3 and x4 in Figure 4); (2) both are in the increment phase\\\\nand each is processing a token at different index from each\\\\nother (x1 and x2); or (3) each request is in the different phase:\\\\ninitiation or increment (x1 and x3). Recall that in order to\\\\nbatch the execution of multiple requests, the execution of each\\\\nrequest must consist of identical operations, each consuming\\\\nidentically-shaped input tensors. In the ﬁrst case, the two\\\\nrequests cannot be processed in a batch because the “length”\\\\ndimension of their input tensors, which is the number of input\\\\ntokens, are not equal. The requests in the second case have\\\\ndifference in the tensor shape of Attention keys and values\\\\nbecause each processes token at different index, as shown in\\\\nFigure 1c. For the third case, we cannot batch the iterations of\\\\ndifferent phases because they take different number of tokens\\\\nas input; an iteration of the initiation phase processes all input\\\\ntokens in parallel for efﬁciency, while in the increment phase\\\\neach iteration takes a single token as its input (we assume the\\\\nuse of fairseq-style incremental decoding [43]).\\\\nBatching is only applicable when the two selected requests\\\\nare in the same phase, with the same number of input tokens\\\\n(in case of the initiation phase) or with the same token index\\\\n(in case of the increment phase). This restriction signiﬁcantly\\\\nreduces the likelihood of batching in real-world workloads,\\\\nUSENIX Association\\\\n16th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation    525\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 7 ---\\\\nQKV Linear\\\\nSplit\\\\nAttention K/V Manager\\\\nAttn x4\\\\nx4\\\\nAttn x3\\\\nx3\\\\nAttn x2\\\\nx2\\\\nAttn x1\\\\nx1\\\\nLayer Input\\\\nKey\\\\nValue\\\\nx1 : (x11, x12, x13)\\\\nx1 : (x11, x12, x13)\\\\nx2 : (x21)\\\\nx2 : (x21)\\\\nMerge\\\\nAttn Out \\\\nLinear\\\\n[7, H]\\\\n[7, H]\\\\n· · ·\\\\n· · ·\\\\n[7, H]\\\\n[7, H]\\\\n[2, 3H]\\\\n[2, 3H]\\\\n[3, 3H]\\\\n[3, 3H]\\\\n[1, 3H]\\\\n[1, 3H]\\\\n[1, 3H]\\\\n[1, 3H]\\\\n[7, 3H]\\\\n[7, 3H]\\\\n[7, H]\\\\n[7, H]\\\\nx32\\\\nx32\\\\nx41\\\\nx41 x42\\\\nx42 x43\\\\nx43\\\\nx14\\\\nx14\\\\nx22\\\\nx22\\\\nx31\\\\nx31\\\\n[2, H]\\\\n[2, H]\\\\n[3, H]\\\\n[3, H]\\\\n[1, H]\\\\n[1, H]\\\\n[1, H]\\\\n[1, H]\\\\nFigure 5: An illustration of ORCA execution engine running\\\\na Transformer layer on a batch of requests with selective\\\\nbatching. We only depict the QKV Linear, Attention, and\\\\nAttention Out Linear operations for simplicity.\\\\nbecause the scheduler should make a wish for the presence\\\\nof two requests eligible for batching at the same time. The\\\\nlikelihood further decreases exponentially as the batch size\\\\nincreases, making it impractical to use a large batch size that\\\\ncan pull out better throughput without compromising latency.\\\\nS2: Selective batching.\\\\nWe propose selective batching, a\\\\ntechnique for batched execution that allows high ﬂexibility in\\\\ncomposing requests as a batch. Instead of processing a batch\\\\nof requests by “batchifying” all tensor operations composing\\\\nthe model, this technique selectively apply batching only to a\\\\nhandful of operations.\\\\nThe main problem regarding batching described above is\\\\nthat the three aforementioned cases4 correspond to irregu-\\\\nlarly shaped input (or state) tensors, which cannot be coa-\\\\nlesced into a single large tensor and fed into a batch opera-\\\\ntion. In the canonical batching mechanism, at each iteration,\\\\na Transformer layer takes a 3-dimensional input tensor of\\\\nshape [B,L,H] generated by concatenating multiple [L,H] in-\\\\nput tensors of requests in a batch, where B is the batch size,\\\\nL is the number of tokens processed together, and H is the\\\\nhidden size of the model. For example, in Figure 3, “iter 1”\\\\n(initiation phase) takes an input tensor of shape [2,2,H] and\\\\n“iter 2” (increment phase) takes a tensor of shape [2,1,H].\\\\nHowever, when the scheduler decides to run an iteration on\\\\nbatch (x1,x2,x3,x4) in Figure 4, the inputs for requests in the\\\\ninitiation phase (x3 : [2,H] and x4 : [3,H]) cannot coalesce\\\\ninto a single tensor of shape [B,L,H] because x3 and x4 have\\\\ndifferent number of input tokens, 2 and 3.\\\\nInterestingly, not all operations are incompatible with such\\\\nirregularly shaped tensors. Operations such as non-Attention\\\\nmatrix multiplication and layer normalization can be made to\\\\nwork with irregularly shaped tensors by ﬂattening the tensors.\\\\n4We use the ﬁrst case as a driving example, but the argument can be\\\\nsimilarly applied to the other two cases.\\\\nFor instance, the aforementioned input tensors for x3 and x4\\\\ncan compose a 2-dimensional tensor of shape [∑L,H] = [5,H]\\\\nwithout an explicit batch dimension. This tensor can be fed\\\\ninto all non-Attention operations including Linear, Layer-\\\\nNorm, Add, and GeLU operations because they do not need to\\\\ndistinguish tensor elements of different requests. On the other\\\\nhand, the Attention operation requires a notion of requests\\\\n(i.e., requires the batch dimension) to compute attention only\\\\nbetween the tokens of the same request, typically done by\\\\napplying cuBLAS routines for batch matrix multiplication.\\\\nSelective batching is aware of the different characteristics\\\\nof each operation; it splits the batch and processes each re-\\\\nquest individually for the Attention operation while applying\\\\ntoken-wise (instead of request-wise) batching to other oper-\\\\nations without the notion of requests. Figure 5 presents the\\\\nselective batching mechanism processing a batch of requests\\\\n(x1,x2,x3,x4) described in Figure 4. This batch has 7 input\\\\ntokens to process, so we make the input tensor have a shape\\\\nof [7,H] and apply the non-Attention operations. Before the\\\\nAttention operation, we insert a Split operation and run the\\\\nAttention operation separately on the split tensor for each\\\\nrequest. The outputs of Attention operations are merged back\\\\ninto a tensor of shape [7,H] by a Merge operation, bringing\\\\nback the batching functionality to the rest of operations.\\\\nTo make the requests in the increment phase can use the\\\\nAttention keys and values for the tokens processed in previous\\\\niterations, ORCA maintains the generated keys and values in\\\\nthe Attention K/V manager. The manager maintains these\\\\nkeys and values separately for each request until the scheduler\\\\nexplicitly asks to remove certain request’s keys and values,\\\\ni.e., when the request has ﬁnished processing. The Attention\\\\noperation for request in the increment phase (x1 and x2) takes\\\\nkeys and values of previous tokens (x11,x12,x13 for x1; x21 for\\\\nx2) from the manager, along with the current token’s query,\\\\nkey, and value from the Split operation to compute attention\\\\nbetween the current token and the previous ones.\\\\n4\\\\nORCA Design\\\\nBased on the above techniques, we design and implement\\\\nORCA: a distributed serving system for Transformer-based\\\\ngenerative models. We have already discussed the system\\\\ncomponents and the overall execution model of ORCA while\\\\ndescribing Figure 4. In this section, we answer the remaining\\\\nissues about how to build an efﬁcient system that can scale to\\\\nlarge-scale models with hundreds of billions of parameters.\\\\nWe also describe the scheduling algorithm for iteration-level\\\\nscheduling, i.e., how to select a batch of requests from the\\\\nrequest pool at every iteration.\\\\n4.1\\\\nDistributed Architecture\\\\nRecent works [12,31] have shown that scaling language mod-\\\\nels can dramatically improve the quality of models. Hence,\\\\n526    16th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation\\\\nUSENIX Association\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 8 ---\\\\nLayer1\\\\nLayer2\\\\nLayer3\\\\nLayer4\\\\nGPU1\\\\nGPU2\\\\nGPU3\\\\nGPU4\\\\nGPU5\\\\nGPU6\\\\nFigure 6: An example of intra- and inter- layer parallelism. A\\\\nvertical dotted line indicates partitioning between layers and\\\\na horizontal line indicates partitioning within a layer.\\\\nExecution Engine\\\\nScheduler\\\\nController\\\\nControl Plane\\\\nData Plane\\\\nWorker 1\\\\nGPU\\\\nGPU\\\\nGPU\\\\nEngine Master\\\\nschedule\\\\ntokens\\\\nController\\\\nWorker 2\\\\nGPU\\\\nGPU\\\\nGPU\\\\ntokens\\\\ncontrol\\\\nmessage\\\\ncontrol\\\\nmessage\\\\ntokens\\\\nFigure 7: An illustration of the distributed architecture of\\\\nORCA’s execution engine using the parallelization conﬁgura-\\\\ntion shown in Figure 6. For example, the ﬁrst inter-layer parti-\\\\ntion (Layer1 and Layer2) in Figure 6 is assigned to Worker1,\\\\nwhile the second partition is assigned to Worker2.\\\\nsystem support for serving such large language models is get-\\\\nting more importance, especially when the model does not ﬁt\\\\nin a single GPU. In such a case, one should split the model\\\\nparameters along with the corresponding computation and\\\\ndistribute them across multiple GPUs and machines.\\\\nORCA composes known parallelization techniques for\\\\nTransformer models: intra-layer parallelism and inter-layer\\\\nparallelism. These two model parallelism strategies, which\\\\nare also used by FasterTransformer [4], have been origi-\\\\nnally developed for distributed training. Intra-layer paral-\\\\nlelism [55,58] splits matrix multiplications (i.e., Linear and\\\\nAttention operations) and their associated parameters over\\\\nmultiple GPUs. We omit the detail about how this strat-\\\\negy partitions each matrix multiplication. On the other hand,\\\\ninter-layer parallelism splits Transformer layers over multiple\\\\nGPUs. ORCA assigns the same number of Transformer layers\\\\nto each GPU. Figure 6 illustrates an example application of\\\\nintra- and inter- layer parallelism to a 4-layer GPT model. The\\\\n4 layers are split into 2 inter-layer partitions, and the layers in\\\\nthe partition are subdivided into 3 intra-layer partitions. We\\\\nassign each partition to a GPU, using a total of 6 GPUs.\\\\nThe ORCA execution engine supports distributed execution\\\\nusing the techniques described above. Figure 7 depicts the\\\\narchitecture of an ORCA engine. Each worker process is re-\\\\nsponsible for an inter-layer partition of the model and can be\\\\nplaced on a different machine from each other. In particular,\\\\neach worker manages one or more CPU threads each dedi-\\\\ncated for controlling a GPU, the number of which depends on\\\\nthe degree of intra-layer parallelism.\\\\nThe execution procedure of the ORCA execution engine is\\\\nas follows. Once the engine is scheduled to run an iteration of\\\\nthe model for a batch of requests, the engine master forwards\\\\nthe received information about the scheduled batch to the ﬁrst\\\\nworker process (Worker1). The information includes tokens\\\\nfor the current iteration and a control message, which is com-\\\\nposed of ids of requests within the batch, current token index\\\\n(for requests in the increment phase), and number of input\\\\ntokens (for requests in the initiation phase). The controller of\\\\nWorker1 hands over the information received from the engine\\\\nmaster to the GPU-controlling threads, where each thread\\\\nparses the information and issues proper GPU kernels to its\\\\nassociated GPU. For example, the kernel for the Attention\\\\noperation uses the request id and the current token index to get\\\\nthe GPU memory address of previous keys and values kept by\\\\nthe Attention K/V manager. In the meantime, the controller\\\\nalso forwards the control message to the controller of the next\\\\nworker (Worker2), without waiting for the completion of the\\\\nkernels issued on the GPUs of Worker1. Unlike Worker1, the\\\\ncontroller of the last worker (Worker2) waits for (i.e., syn-\\\\nchronize with) the completion of the issued GPU kernels, in\\\\norder to fetch the output token for each request and send the\\\\ntokens back to the engine master.\\\\nTo keep GPUs busy as much as possible, we design the\\\\nORCA engine to minimize synchronization between the CPU\\\\nand GPUs. We observe that current systems for distributed\\\\ninference (e.g., FasterTransformer [4] and Megatron-LM [3])\\\\nhave CPU-GPU synchronization whenever each process re-\\\\nceives control messages5 because they exchange the messages\\\\nthrough a GPU-to-GPU communication channel – NCCL [5].\\\\nThe exchange of these control messages occurs at every iter-\\\\nation, imposing a non-negligible performance overhead. On\\\\nthe other hand, ORCA separates the communication channels\\\\nfor control messages (plus tokens) and tensor data transfer,\\\\navoiding the use of NCCL for data used by CPUs. Figure 7\\\\nshows that the ORCA engine uses NCCL exclusively for ex-\\\\nchanging intermediate tensor data (represented by dashed\\\\narrows) as this data is produced and consumed by GPUs. Con-\\\\ntrol messages, which is used by the CPU threads for issuing\\\\nGPU kernels, sent between the engine master and worker con-\\\\ntrollers by a separate communication channel that does not\\\\ninvolve GPU such as gRPC [2].\\\\n4.2\\\\nScheduling Algorithm\\\\nThe ORCA scheduler makes decisions on which requests\\\\nshould be selected and processed at every iteration. The sched-\\\\nuler has high ﬂexibility in selecting a set of requests to com-\\\\n5This includes various metadata such as batch size, sequence length, and\\\\nwhether a request within the batch has ﬁnished processing.\\\\nUSENIX Association\\\\n16th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation    527\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 9 ---\\\\npose a batch, because of the selective batching technique that\\\\nallows the engine to run any set of requests in the batched\\\\nmanner. Now the main question left is how to select the re-\\\\nquests at every iteration.\\\\nWe design the ORCA scheduler to use a simple algorithm\\\\nthat does not change the processing order of client requests;\\\\nearly-arrived requests are processed earlier. That is, we en-\\\\nsure iteration-level ﬁrst-come-ﬁrst-served (FCFS) property.\\\\nWe deﬁne the iteration-level FCFS property for workloads\\\\nwith multi-iteration characteristics as follows: for any pair\\\\nof requests (xi,xj) in the request pool, if xi has arrived ear-\\\\nlier than x j, xi should have run the same or more iterations\\\\nthan xj. Note that some late-arrived requests may return ear-\\\\nlier to clients if the late request requires a smaller number of\\\\niterations to ﬁnish.\\\\nStill, the scheduler needs to take into account additional\\\\nfactors: diminishing returns to increasing the batch size and\\\\nGPU memory constraint. Increasing the batch size trades off\\\\nincreased throughput for increased latency, but as the batch\\\\nsize becomes larger, the amount of return (i.e., increase in\\\\nthroughput) diminishes. Therefore, just like other serving sys-\\\\ntems [7,16], ORCA also has a notion of a max batch size: the\\\\nlargest possible number of requests within a batch. The ORCA\\\\nsystem operator can tune this knob to maximize throughput\\\\nwhile satisfying one’s latency budget. We will discuss this in\\\\nmore details with experiment results in Section 6.2.\\\\nAnother factor is the GPU memory constraint. Optimiz-\\\\ning memory usage by reusing buffers for intermediate results\\\\nacross multiple operations is a well-known technique used by\\\\nvarious systems [4,6], and ORCA also adopts this technique.\\\\nHowever, unlike the buffers for intermediate results that can\\\\nbe reused immediately, buffers used by the Attention K/V\\\\nmanager for storing the keys and values cannot be reclaimed\\\\nuntil the ORCA scheduler notiﬁes that the corresponding re-\\\\nquest has ﬁnished processing. A naïve implementation can\\\\nmake the scheduler fall into a deadlock when the scheduler\\\\ncannot issue an iteration for any requests in the pool because\\\\nthere is no space left for storing a new Attention key and value\\\\nfor the next token. This requires the ORCA scheduler to be\\\\naware of the remaining size of pre-allocated memory regions\\\\nfor the manager.\\\\nThe ORCA scheduler takes all these factors into account:\\\\nit selects at most “max batch size” requests based on the ar-\\\\nrival time, while reserving enough space for storing keys and\\\\nvalues to a request when the request is scheduled for the ﬁrst\\\\ntime. We describe the scheduling process in Algorithm 1. The\\\\nalgorithm selects a batch of requests from the request pool\\\\n(line 4) and schedules the batch (line 5). The Select function\\\\n(line 17) selects at most max_bs requests from the pool based\\\\non the arrival time of the request (lines 20-22). Algorithm 1\\\\ndoes not depict the procedure of request arrival and return;\\\\none may think of it as there exist concurrent threads insert-\\\\ning newly arrived requests into request_pool and removing\\\\nﬁnished requests from request_pool.\\\\nAlgorithm 1: ORCA scheduling algorithm\\\\nParams: n_workers: number of workers, max_bs:\\\\nmax batch size, n_slots: number of K/V slots\\\\n1 n_scheduled ←0\\\\n2 n_rsrv ←0\\\\n3 while true do\\\\n4\\\\nbatch,n_rsrv ←Select(request_pool,n_rsrv)\\\\n5\\\\nschedule engine to run one iteration of\\\\nthe model for the batch\\\\n6\\\\nforeach req in batch do\\\\n7\\\\nreq.state ←RUNNING\\\\n8\\\\nn_scheduled ←n_scheduled +1\\\\n9\\\\nif n_scheduled = n_workers then\\\\n10\\\\nwait for return of a scheduled batch\\\\n11\\\\nforeach req in the returned batch do\\\\n12\\\\nreq.state ←INCREMENT\\\\n13\\\\nif ﬁnished(req) then\\\\n14\\\\nn_rsrv ←n_rsrv−req.max_tokens\\\\n15\\\\nn_scheduled ←n_scheduled −1\\\\n16\\\\n17 def Select(pool, n_rsrv):\\\\n18\\\\nbatch ←{}\\\\n19\\\\npool ←{req ∈pool|req.state ̸= RUNNING}\\\\n20\\\\nSortByArrivalTime(pool)\\\\n21\\\\nforeach req in pool do\\\\n22\\\\nif batch.size() = max_bs then break\\\\n23\\\\nif req.state = INITIATION then\\\\n24\\\\nnew_n_rsrv ←n_rsrv+req.max_tokens\\\\n25\\\\nif new_n_rsrv > n_slots then break\\\\n26\\\\nn_rsrv ←new_n_rsrv\\\\n27\\\\nbatch ←batchS{req}\\\\n28\\\\nreturn batch,n_rsrv\\\\nWhen the scheduler considers a request in the initiation\\\\nphase, meaning that the request has never been scheduled\\\\nyet, the scheduler uses the request’s max_tokens6 attribute\\\\nto reserve max_tokens slots of GPU memory for storing the\\\\nkeys and values in advance (lines 23-26). That\\\\nis, the operator can simply use the largest possible n_slots\\\\nunder the memory constraint.\\\\nPipeline parallelism.\\\\nORCA’s scheduler makes the execu-\\\\ntion of workers in the engine to be pipelined across multi-\\\\nple batches. The scheduler does not wait for the return of a\\\\nscheduled batch until n_scheduled, the number of currently\\\\nscheduled batches, reaches n_workers (line 9-10 of Algo-\\\\nrithm 1). By doing so, the scheduler keeps the number of\\\\nconcurrently running batches in the engine to be n_workers,\\\\nwhich means that every worker in the engine is processing\\\\none of the batches without being idle.\\\\nFigure 8a depicts the execution pipeline of 3 ORCA work-\\\\ners, using a max batch size of 2. We assume that the request\\\\nA arrives before B, which arrives before C, and so on. At ﬁrst,\\\\nthe scheduler selects requests A and B based on the arrival\\\\ntime and schedules the engine to process a batch of requests\\\\nA and B (we call this batch AB), where Worker1, Worker2,\\\\nand Worker3 process the batch in turn. The scheduler waits\\\\nfor the return of the batch AB only after the scheduler injects\\\\ntwo more batches: CD and EF. Once the batch AB returns,\\\\nrequests A and B get selected and scheduled once again, be-\\\\ncause they are the earliest arrived requests among the requests\\\\nin the pool.\\\\nIn contrast, the interface between current serving systems\\\\nand execution engines (e.g., a combination of Triton [7]\\\\nand FasterTransformer [4]) does not allow injecting another\\\\nbatch before the ﬁnish of the current running batch, due to\\\\nthe request-level scheduling. That is, Triton cannot inject\\\\nthe next request C to FasterTransformer until the current\\\\n# Params\\\\n# Layers\\\\nHidden\\\\nsize\\\\n# Inter-\\\\npartitions\\\\n# Intra-\\\\npartitions\\\\n13B\\\\n40\\\\n5120\\\\n1\\\\n1\\\\n101B\\\\n80\\\\n10240\\\\n1\\\\n8\\\\n175B\\\\n96\\\\n12288\\\\n2\\\\n8\\\\n341B\\\\n120\\\\n15360\\\\n4\\\\n8\\\\nTable 1: Conﬁgurations of models used in the experiments.\\\\nbatch AB ﬁnishes. To enable pipelined execution of multiple\\\\ninter-layer partitions under such constraint, FasterTransformer\\\\nsplits a batch of requests into multiple microbatches [28] and\\\\npipelines the executions of partitions across the microbatches.\\\\nIn Figure 8b, FasterTransformer splits the batch AB into two\\\\nmicrobatches, A and B. Since each partition processes a mi-\\\\ncrobatch (which is smaller than the original batch) in the\\\\nbatched manner, the performance gain from batching can\\\\nbecome smaller. Moreover, this method may insert bubbles\\\\ninto the pipeline when the microbatch size is too large, mak-\\\\ning the number of microbatches smaller than the number of\\\\npartitions. While FasterTransformer needs to trade batching\\\\nefﬁciency (larger microbatch size) for pipelining efﬁciency\\\\n(fewer pipeline bubbles), ORCA is free of such a tradeoff –\\\\nthanks to iteration-level scheduling – and can easily pipeline\\\\nrequests without dividing a batch into microbatches.\\\\n5\\\\nImplementation\\\\nWe have implemented ORCA with 13K lines of C++, based\\\\non the CUDA ecosystem. We use gRPC [2] for the com-\\\\nmunication in the control plane of the ORCA engine, while\\\\nNCCL [5] is used in the data plane, for both inter-layer and\\\\nintra-layer communication. Since we design ORCA to fo-\\\\ncus on Transformer-based generative models, ORCA pro-\\\\nvides popular Transformer layers as a building block of mod-\\\\nels including the original encoder-decoder Transformer [60],\\\\nGPT [47], and other variants discussed in Raffel et al. [49].\\\\nWe have also implemented fused kernels for LayerNorm,\\\\nAttention, and GeLU operators, just like other systems for\\\\ntraining or inference of Transformer models [1, 4, 58]. For\\\\nexample, the procedure of computing dot products between\\\\nAttention query and keys, Softmax on the dot products, and\\\\nweighted average of Attention values are fused into a single\\\\nCUDA kernel for the Attention operator. In addition, we go\\\\none step further and fuse the kernels of the split Attention\\\\noperators by simply concatenating all thread blocks of the\\\\nkernels for different requests. Although this fusion makes the\\\\nthread blocks within a kernel have different characteristics and\\\\nlifetimes (which is often discouraged by CUDA programming\\\\npractice) because they process tensors of different shapes, we\\\\nﬁnd this fusion to be beneﬁcial by improving GPU utilization\\\\nand reducing the kernel launch overhead [34,39].\\\\nUSENIX Association\\\\n16th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation    529\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 11 ---\\\\n6\\\\nEvaluation\\\\nIn this section, we present evaluation results to show the\\\\nefﬁciency of ORCA.\\\\nEnvironment.\\\\nWe run our evaluation on Azure ND96asr\\\\nA100 v4 VMs, each equipped with 8 NVIDIA 40-GB A100\\\\nGPUs connected over NVLink. We use at most four VMs\\\\ndepending on the size of the model being tested. Each VM\\\\nhas 8 Mellanox 200Gbps HDR Inﬁniband adapters, providing\\\\nan 1.6Tb/s of interconnect bandwidth between VMs.\\\\nModels.\\\\nThroughout the experiments, we use GPT [12] as a\\\\nrepresentative example of Transformer-based generative mod-\\\\nels. We use GPT models with various conﬁgurations, which is\\\\nlisted in Table 1. The conﬁgurations for 13B and 175B models\\\\ncome from the GPT-3 paper [12]. Based on these two mod-\\\\nels, we change the number of layers and hidden size to make\\\\nconﬁgurations for 101B and 341B models. All models have\\\\na maximum sequence length of 2048, following the setting\\\\nof the original literature [12]. We use fp16-formatted model\\\\nparameters and intermediate activations for the experiments.\\\\nWe also apply inter- and intra- layer parallelism strategies\\\\ndescribed in Section 4.1, except for the 13B model that can ﬁt\\\\nin a GPU. For example, the 175B model is partitioned over a\\\\ntotal of 16 GPUs by using 2 inter-layer partitions subdivided\\\\ninto 8 intra-layer partitions, where the 8 GPUs in the same\\\\nVM belongs to the same inter-layer partition.\\\\nBaseline system.\\\\nWe compare with FasterTransformer [4],\\\\nan inference engine that supports large scale Transformer\\\\nmodels via distributed execution. While there exist other\\\\nsystems with the support for distributed execution such as\\\\nMegatron-LM [3] and DeepSpeed [1], these systems are pri-\\\\nmarily designed and optimized for training workloads, which\\\\nmakes them show relatively lower performance compared to\\\\nthe inference-optimized systems.\\\\nScenarios.\\\\nWe use two different scenarios to drive our eval-\\\\nuation. First, we design a microbenchmark to solely assess the\\\\nperformance of the ORCA engine without being affected by\\\\nthe iteration-level scheduling. In particular, we do not run the\\\\nORCA scheduler in this scenario. Instead, given a batch of re-\\\\nquests, the testing script repeats injecting the same batch into\\\\nthe ORCA engine until all requests in the batch ﬁnishes, mim-\\\\nicking the behavior of the canonical request-level scheduling.\\\\nWe also assume that all requests in the batch have the same\\\\nnumber of input tokens and generate the same number of\\\\noutput tokens. We report the time taken for processing the\\\\nbatch (not individual requests) and compare the result with\\\\nFasterTransformer [4].\\\\nThe second scenario tests the end-to-end performance of\\\\nORCA by emulating a workload. We synthesize a trace of\\\\nclient requests because there is no publicly-available request\\\\ntrace for generative language models. Each request in the syn-\\\\nthesized trace is randomly generated by sampling the number\\\\nof input tokens and a max_gen_tokens attribute, where the\\\\nnumber of input tokens plus max_gen_tokens equals to the\\\\nmax_tokens attribute described in Section 4.2. We assume\\\\nthat all requests continue generation until the number of gen-\\\\nerated tokens reaches max_gen_tokens. In other words, we\\\\nmake the model never emit the “<EOS>” token. This is be-\\\\ncause we have neither the actual model checkpoint nor the\\\\nactual input text so we do not have any information to guess\\\\nthe right timing of the “<EOS>” token generation. Once the\\\\nrequests are generated, we synthesize the trace by setting the\\\\nrequest arrival time based on the Poisson process. To assess\\\\nORCA’s behavior under varying load, we change the Poisson\\\\nparameter (i.e., arrival rate) and adjust the request arrival time\\\\naccordingly. We report latency and throughput using mul-\\\\ntiple traces generated from different distributions for better\\\\ncomparison and understanding of the behavior of ORCA and\\\\nFasterTransformer.\\\\n6.1\\\\nEngine Microbenchmark\\\\nWe ﬁrst compare the performance of FasterTransformer and\\\\nthe ORCA engine using the ﬁrst scenario. We set all requests\\\\nin the batch to have the same number of input tokens (32 or\\\\n128) and generate 32 tokens. That is, in this set of experiments,\\\\nall requests within the batch start and ﬁnish processing at the\\\\nsame time. We conduct experiments using three different\\\\nmodels: 13B, 101B, and 175B. For each model, we use the\\\\ncorresponding parallelization strategy shown in Table 1.\\\\nFigure 9 shows the performance of FasterTransformer and\\\\nthe ORCA engine for processing a batch composed of the same\\\\nrequests. In Figure 9a, the ORCA engine shows a similar (or\\\\nslightly worse) performance compared to FasterTransformer\\\\nacross all conﬁgurations. This is because ORCA does not\\\\napply batching to the Attention operations, while FasterTrans-\\\\nformer apply batching to all operations. Still, the performance\\\\ndifference is relatively small. Despite not batching the Atten-\\\\ntion operation, the absence of model parameters in Attention\\\\nmakes this decision has little impact on efﬁciency as there\\\\nis no beneﬁt of reusing model parameters across multiple\\\\nrequests.\\\\nFigure 9b presents similar results for the 101B model that\\\\nuses all of the 8 GPUs in a single VM. From these results, we\\\\ncan say that the ORCA engine and FasterTransformer have\\\\ncomparable efﬁciencies in the implementations of CUDA\\\\nkernels and the communication between intra-layer partitions.\\\\nNote that FasterTransformer cannot use a batch size of 8 or\\\\nlarger with the 13B model (16 or larger with the 101B model)\\\\nbecause of the ﬁxed amount of memory pre-allocation for\\\\neach request’s Attention keys and values, which grows in\\\\nproportion to the max sequence length of the model (2048\\\\nfor this case). In contrast, ORCA avoids redundant memory\\\\n530    16th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation\\\\nUSENIX Association\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 12 ---\\\\n1\\\\n2\\\\n4\\\\n8\\\\n16\\\\n32\\\\nBatch Size\\\\n0\\\\n500\\\\n1000\\\\n1500\\\\nExecution Time (ms)\\\\nft(32)\\\\norca(32)\\\\nft(128)\\\\norca(128)\\\\n(a) 13B model, 1 GPU.\\\\n1\\\\n2\\\\n4\\\\n8\\\\n16\\\\n32\\\\nBatch Size\\\\n0\\\\n1000\\\\n2000\\\\nExecution Time (ms)\\\\nft(32)\\\\norca(32)\\\\nft(128)\\\\norca(128)\\\\n(b) 101B model, 8 GPUs.\\\\n1\\\\n2\\\\n4\\\\n8\\\\n16\\\\n32\\\\nBatch Size\\\\n0\\\\n1000\\\\n2000\\\\n3000\\\\nExecution Time (ms)\\\\nft(32)\\\\norca(32)\\\\nft(128)\\\\norca(128)\\\\n(c) 175B model, 16 GPUs.\\\\nFigure 9: Execution time of a batch of requests using FasterTransformer and the ORCA engine without the scheduling component.\\\\nLabel “ft(n)” represents results from FasterTransformer processing requests with n input tokens. For Faster-\\\\nTransformer, we set the size of a microbatch to be equal to the\\\\nbatch size to disable pipelining. As shown in Figure 9c, the\\\\nORCA engine outperforms FasterTransformer by up to 47%.\\\\nWe attribute this performance improvement to the control-\\\\ndata plane separation described in Section 4.1. We omit the\\\\n341B model as it has similar results compared to the 175B\\\\nmodel.\\\\n6.2\\\\nEnd-to-end Performance\\\\nNow we assess the end-to-end performance of ORCA by\\\\nmeasuring the latency and throughput with the synthesized\\\\nrequest trace under varying load. When synthesizing the\\\\ntrace, we sample each request’s number of input tokens from\\\\nU(32,512), a uniform distribution ranging from 32 to 512\\\\n(inclusive). The max_gen_tokens attributed is sampled from\\\\nU(1,128), which means that the least and the most time-\\\\nconsuming requests require 1 and 128 iterations of the model\\\\nfor processing, respectively.\\\\nUnlike the microbenchmark shown in Section 6.1, to mea-\\\\nsure the end-to-end performance, we test the entire ORCA\\\\nsoftware stack including the ORCA scheduler. Client requests\\\\narrive to the ORCA scheduler following the synthesized trace\\\\ndescribed above. We report results from various max batch\\\\nsize conﬁgurations. For FasterTransformer that does not have\\\\nits own scheduler, we implement a custom scheduler that re-\\\\nceives client requests, creates batches, and injects the batches\\\\nto an instance of FasterTransformer. We make the custom\\\\nscheduler create batches dynamically by taking at most max\\\\nbatch size requests from the request queue, which is the most\\\\ncommon scheduling algorithm used by existing serving sys-\\\\ntems like Triton [7] and TensorFlow Serving [42]. Again,\\\\nwe report results from various max batch size conﬁgurations,\\\\nalong with varying microbatch sizes, an additional knob in\\\\nFasterTransformer that governs the pipelining behavior (see\\\\nSection 4.2).\\\\nFigure 10 shows median end-to-end latency and throughput.\\\\nSince each request in the trace requires different processing\\\\ntime, which is (roughly) in proportion to the number of gener-\\\\nated tokens, we report median latency normalized by the num-\\\\nber of generated tokens of each request. From the ﬁgure, we\\\\ncan see that ORCA provides signiﬁcantly higher throughput\\\\nand lower latency than FasterTransformer. The only excep-\\\\ntion is the 101B model under low load (Figure 10a). In this\\\\nUSENIX Association\\\\n16th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation    531\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 13 ---\\\\n0\\\\n5\\\\n10\\\\n15\\\\n20\\\\nThroughput (req/s)\\\\n103\\\\n104\\\\nLatency (ms)\\\\nft(1, 1)\\\\nft(8, 8)\\\\norca(1)\\\\norca(8)\\\\norca(16)\\\\norca(32)\\\\n(a) (# in, # gen) = (32, 32)\\\\n0.0\\\\n0.5\\\\n1.0\\\\n1.5\\\\n2.0\\\\n2.5\\\\n3.0\\\\nThroughput (req/s)\\\\n104\\\\n105\\\\nLatency (ms)\\\\nft(1, 1)\\\\nft(8, 8)\\\\norca(1)\\\\norca(8)\\\\norca(16)\\\\norca(32)\\\\n(b) (# in, # gen) = (256, 256)\\\\nFigure 11: Median end-to-end latency and throughput, using\\\\nthe 175B model with traces composed of homogeneous re-\\\\nquests. We do not normalize the latency since all requests\\\\nhave the same characteristic.\\\\ncase, both ORCA and FasterTransformer do not have enough\\\\nnumber of requests to process in a batch. That is, the latency\\\\nwill mostly depend on the engine’s performance, which is\\\\nshown in Figure 9b. As the load becomes heavier, ORCA\\\\nprovides higher throughput with a relatively small increase\\\\nin latency, because the ORCA scheduler makes late-arrived\\\\nrequests hitch a ride with the current ongoing batch. In con-\\\\ntrast, FasterTransformer fails to efﬁciently handle multiple\\\\nrequests that (1) arrive at different times; (2) require differ-\\\\nent number of iterations to ﬁnish; or (3) start with different\\\\nnumber of input tokens, resulting in a peak throughput of 0.49\\\\nreq/s and much higher latency. If we use the 175B or 341B\\\\nmodel (Figures 10b and 10c) that employs more than one\\\\ninter-layer partitions, ORCA outperforms FasterTransformer\\\\nunder every level of load in terms of both latency and through-\\\\nput, resulting in an order of magnitude higher throughput\\\\nwhen we compare results at a similar level of latency. For\\\\nexample, to match a median normalized latency of 190ms for\\\\nthe 175B model, which is a double of the normalized execu-\\\\ntion time (by the number of generated tokens) of “orca(128)”\\\\nshown in Figure 9c, FasterTransformer provides a throughput\\\\nof 0.185 req/s whereas ORCA provides a throughput of 6.81\\\\nreq/s, which is a 36.9× speedup.\\\\nVarying batch size conﬁgurations.\\\\nFigure 10 shows that\\\\nthe increase of the max batch size of ORCA results in a higher\\\\nthroughput without affecting the latency. This is because the\\\\niteration-level scheduling of ORCA resolves the problem of\\\\nearly-ﬁnished and late-joining requests. Nevertheless, there is\\\\nno guarantee that increasing the batch size will not negatively\\\\naffect the latency, for arbitrary hardware settings, models, and\\\\nworkloads. As mentioned in Section 4.2, the max batch size\\\\nmust be set carefully by considering both the required latency\\\\nand throughput requirements.\\\\nInterestingly, larger max batch size in FasterTransformer\\\\ndoes not necessarily help improving throughput. By testing\\\\nall possible combinations of max batch size (max_bs) and\\\\nmicrobatch size (mbs) on all models under varying load, we\\\\nﬁnd that (max_bs, mbs) = (1, 1) or (8, 8) are the best op-\\\\ntions. Per our discussion in Section 4.1, FasterTransformer’s\\\\nmicrobatch-based pipelining can be less efﬁcient because the\\\\nengine is going to process at most mbs number of requests\\\\nin the batched manner, which explains why the conﬁgura-\\\\ntions with the maximum possible mbs (which is the same\\\\nas max_bs) have better performance than others. In addition,\\\\nwhile increasing max_bs can improve performance due to the\\\\nincreased batch size, at the same time, this also increases the\\\\nlikelihood of batching requests with large difference in the\\\\nnumber of input tokens or the number of generated tokens. In\\\\nsuch cases, FasterTransformer cannot efﬁciently handle the\\\\nbatch because (1) for the ﬁrst iteration of the batch, Faster-\\\\nTransformer processes requests as if they all had the same\\\\ninput length as the shortest one; and (2) early-ﬁnished requests\\\\ncannot immediately return to the clients.\\\\nTrace of homogeneous requests.\\\\nWe test the behavior of\\\\nORCA and FasterTransformer when using a trace of homoge-\\\\nneous requests, i.e., all requests in a trace have the same num-\\\\nber of input tokens and the same max_gen_tokens attribute.\\\\nSince all requests require the same number of iterations to\\\\nﬁnish processing, the problem of early-leaving requests does\\\\nnot occur for this trace. As a result, now the increase of the\\\\nmax_bs has a noticeable positive impact on the performance\\\\nof FasterTransformer, as shown in Figure 11. Still, ORCA out-\\\\nperforms FasterTransformer (max_bs=8) except for the case\\\\nusing a max batch size of 1, where ORCA degenerates into a\\\\nsimple pipeline of the ORCA workers that does not perform\\\\nbatching.\\\\n7\\\\nRelated Work and Discussion\\\\nFine-grained batching for recurrent models.\\\\nWe would\\\\nlike to highlight BatchMaker [23] as one of the most relevant\\\\nprevious works. BatchMaker is a serving system for RNNs\\\\nthat performs scheduling and batching at the granularity of\\\\nRNN cells, motivated by the unique RNN characteristic of re-\\\\npeating the same computation. Once a request arrives, Batch-\\\\nMaker breaks the dataﬂow graph for processing the request\\\\ninto RNN cells, schedules execution at the granularity of cells\\\\n(instead of the entire graph), and batches the execution of iden-\\\\ntical cells (if any). Since each RNN cell always performs the\\\\nexact same computation, BatchMaker can execute multiple\\\\nRNN cells in a batched manner regardless of the position (i.e.,\\\\ntoken index) of the cell. By doing so, BatchMaker allows a\\\\nnewly arrived request for RNN to join (or a ﬁnished request\\\\n532    16th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation\\\\nUSENIX Association\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 14 ---\\\\nto leave) the current executing batch without waiting for the\\\\nbatch to completely ﬁnish.\\\\nHowever, BatchMaker cannot make batches of cells for\\\\nTransformer models because there are too many distinct cells\\\\n(a subgraph that encapsulates the computation for processing\\\\na token; Figure 1c) in the graph. Each cell at a different to-\\\\nken index t must use a different set of Attention Keys/Values.\\\\nAs the cell for each t is different, the graph comprises L dif-\\\\nferent cells (L denotes the number of input and generated\\\\ntokens), signiﬁcantly lowering the likelihood of cells of the\\\\nsame computation being present at a given moment (e.g., in\\\\nFigure 10, L ranges from 33 = 32 + 1 to 640 = 512 + 128).\\\\nThus execution of the cells will be mostly serialized, making\\\\nBatchMaker fall back to non-batched execution. BatchMaker\\\\nalso lacks support for large models that require model and\\\\npipeline parallelism.\\\\nWhile BatchMaker is geared towards detecting and aligning\\\\nbatch-able RNN cells, our key principle in designing ORCA is\\\\nto perform as much computation as possible per each round of\\\\nmodel parameter read. This is based on the insight that reading\\\\nparameters from GPU global memory is a major bottleneck\\\\nin terms of end-to-end execution time, for large-scale models.\\\\nAdhering to this principle, we apply iteration-level scheduling\\\\nand selective batching to process all “ready” tokens in a single\\\\nround of parameter read, regardless of whether the processing\\\\nof tokens can be batched (non-Attention ops) or not (Attention\\\\nops).\\\\nSpecialized execution engines for Transformer models.\\\\nThe outstanding performance of Transformer-based models\\\\nencourages the development of inference systems specialized\\\\nfor them. FasterTransformer [4], LightSeq [61], TurboTrans-\\\\nformers [22] and EET [36] are such examples. Each of these\\\\nsystems behave as an backend execution engine of existing\\\\nserving systems like Triton Inference Server [7] and Tensor-\\\\nFlow Serving [42]. That is, these systems delegate the role\\\\nof scheduling to the serving system layer, adhering to the\\\\ncanonical request-level scheduling. Instead, ORCA suggests\\\\nto schedule executions at a ﬁner granularity, which is not pos-\\\\nsible in current systems without changing the mechanism for\\\\ncoordination between the scheduler and the execution engine.\\\\nNote that among these systems, FasterTransformer is the only\\\\none with the support for distributed execution. While systems\\\\nlike Megatron-LM [3] and DeepSpeed [1] can also be used for\\\\ndistributed execution, these systems are primarily optimized\\\\nfor large-scale training rather than inference serving.\\\\nInterface between serving systems and execution engines.\\\\nCurrent general-purpose serving systems such as Triton In-\\\\nference Server [7] and Clipper [16] serve as an abstraction\\\\nfor handling client requests and scheduling executions of the\\\\nunderlying execution engines. This approach is found to be\\\\nbeneﬁcial by separating the design and implementation of\\\\nthe serving layer and the execution layer. However, we ﬁnd\\\\nthat the prevalent interface between the two layers is too re-\\\\nstricted for handling models like GPT [12], which has the\\\\nmulti-iteration characteristic. Instead, we design ORCA to\\\\ntightly integrate the scheduler and the engine, simplifying the\\\\napplication of the two proposed techniques: iteration-level\\\\nscheduling and selective batching. While in this paper we\\\\ndo not study a general interface design that supports the two\\\\ntechniques without losing the separation of abstractions, it\\\\ncan be an interesting topic to explore such possibility; we\\\\nleave this issue to future work.\\\\n8\\\\nConclusion\\\\nWe present iteration-level scheduling with selective batch-\\\\ning, a novel approach that achieves low latency and high\\\\nthroughput for serving Transformer-based generative mod-\\\\nels. Iteration-level scheduling makes the scheduler interact\\\\nwith the execution engine at the granularity of iteration in-\\\\nstead of request, while selective batching enables batching\\\\narbitrary requests processing tokens at different positions,\\\\nwhich is crucial for applying batching with iteration-level\\\\nscheduling. Based on these techniques, we have designed\\\\nand implemented a distributed serving system named ORCA.\\\\nExperiments show the effectiveness of our approach: ORCA\\\\nprovides an order of magnitude higher throughput than current\\\\nstate-of-the-art systems at the same level of latency.\\\\nAcknowledgments\\\\nWe thank our shepherd Amar Phanishayee and the anony-\\\\nmous reviewers for their insightful comments.
